newsitem.title: USA: California's Sun Diamond on trial in Espy probe.
newsitem.headline: California's Sun Diamond on trial in Espy probe.

text.p: The first trial stemming from the criminal probe of former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy opens on Monday, marking a new phase of a sweeping investigation that could embarrass the White House.

On trial will be one of the nation's largest agricultural cooperatives, Sun Diamond Growers of California, which has been charged with illegally trying to influence Espy while he was Agriculture Secretary with expensive gifts and favors.

The giant fruit cooperative, whose affiliates include Sun Maid raisins, Sunsweet prunes and Diamond Walnut, has also been accused of making illegal campaign contributions to Espy's brother Henry, and of wire fraud.
The charges have arisen out of a sprawling two-year, $5 million-plus criminal investigation of Espy being conducted by Independent Counsel Donald Smaltz.

Espy, a former Mississipi congressman, left the huge Agriculture Department in 1994 amid a swirl of accusations that he had improperly accepted gratuities from companies and concerns his agency regulated.

So far the probe has returned four sets of criminal indictments against a dozen individuals and concerns, including the nation's second largest crop insurance company, and Henry Espy, the former secretary's brother. Henry Espy is scheduled to go on trial in New Orleans in November.
Legal experts watching the progress of the investigation have said the returned indictments appear to be drawing a tighter circle around the former cabinet secretary.
"The chances of Espy getting indicted get greater as each one of these indictments have come in," said Georgetown University law professor Paul Rothstein.

And still being looked into are allegations that the giant Arkansas-based poultry processor Tysons Foods -- which has enjoyed close ties with President Bill Clinton since he was Arkansas governor -- gave gifts to Espy to dissuade him from slapping new regulations on the poultry industry.

The Sun Diamond trial will be closely watched to see how a jury and judge interpret the government's illegal gratuity charges, and if the defense stand that the independent counsel has improperly over-reached his mandate will be successful.
Sources close to the case said whatever the outcome, Smaltz and his team will aggressively push on with the probe.

Other legal experts said a win would be an important psychological victory for the government and could persuade reluctant witnesses to cooperate in other indictments, but that a loss would not bode well for the prosecution.
"If the government wins, it could spur the prosecutorial effort a thousand fold," said Georgetown's Rothstein.
"But if they lose," he said, "they're deprived of what is always one of the main reasons for bringing these cases down lower in the chain -- to get people to snitch on other people."
The trial will pit two of Washington's top lawyers against each other.

Heading the defense team is Richard Hibey, a well known defense attorney who has represented high profile clients such as former Phillipine first lady Imelda Marcos and Jonathan Pollard who pleaded guilty to spying for Israel in the 1980's.

Leading the prosecution's efforts will be Theodore Greenberg, a longtime Justice Department lawyer who headed the Justice's Money Laundering and Fraud Sections and has extensive experience in prosecuting white collar crimes.
"This should be one heck of a face-off," said former U.S. prosecutor Joseph di Genova. "They're both superb lawyers."

Sun Diamond, acting through its Washington lobbyist and longtime Espy friend Richard Douglas, is charged with spending more than $9,000 on Espy for gifts that included tickets and a limousine to the 1993 U.S. Open tennis tournament, and with spending thousands more on Espy's girlfriend.
The defense says the gifts were not to gain favors, but stemmed from the Espy-Douglas friendship.
Controversy first arose around Espy when it was learned he had accepted trips and sports tickets from Tysons Foods while his agency was considering new poultry industry regulations.
Tysons chairman Don Tyson has been a long political supporter of Clinton, and there were rumblings the company was trying to use its clout to soften any planned crackdown.
Tysons officials have consistently denied charges that they ever tried to influence the administration.
